title: The Container Revolution 📦
description: Discover why Docker was created and how containers solve the “works on my machine” problem.

slides.title: The Problem Docker Solves 🚢
slides.content:
# The Shipping Container Analogy

Before shipping containers, every piece of cargo had to be handled individually. Ships, trains and trucks were all incompatible.

**Software development has the same chaos!**

*   Your app works on your laptop, but not on the server.
*   Different versions of Python, Node.js or libraries clash.
*   Setting up environments manually is slow and error‑prone.

Docker introduces **standardised containers** – lightweight, portable units that hold your application and everything it needs to run.

> “Build once, run anywhere.”

quizData.question: Which real‑world problem inspired Docker’s design?
quizData.explanation: The shipping container analogy is central to Docker. Just like a container can be moved between ships, trains and trucks without unpacking, a Docker container runs the same way anywhere.

slides.title: What Exactly is a Container? 📦
slides.content:
# A Container Is…

- A **lightweight, stand‑alone, executable package** of software.
- It includes **everything needed to run**: code, runtime, system tools, libraries and settings.
- Containers are **isolated** from each other and the host, but share the OS kernel.

## Key Benefits

- **Portability** – run the same container on any Linux, Windows, or macOS host that has Docker.
- **Speed** – containers start in milliseconds (vs. minutes for VMs).
- **Efficiency** – you can run many more containers than virtual machines on the same hardware.
- **Consistency** – no more “works on my machine” bugs.

quizData.question: True or False: A Docker container includes its own full operating system like a virtual machine.
quizData.explanation: Containers share the host’s OS kernel. They do not include a full guest OS, which makes them much smaller and faster than VMs.

slides.title: Did You Know? 💡
slides.content:
## Fun Fact

The term **container** in computing was first used by Sun Microsystems in the 1990s. Docker popularised the concept by making it developer‑friendly.
